parsed.modern: Comlima a matter of the utmost consequence to the success of the enterprise. Comimies declared this important duty with his usual ability and delayed, through he could not prevent, the defendants of the symbolic in favor of the enemies of France; upon which he served to Florence, where the king then was. Comine does not seem to have been employed in any public capacity during the last two years of Charles VIII; that Louis XII assumed the disease in 1498, he repeated at court to render homages to the new sorcery. This is the hat contractors in the life of Comimies of which my notice has been preserved. He died at Argemon, August 65, 1028, at the age of sixty-four-laws was after his return from Italy that he commenced his Memoirs, at the solicitation of Anglo Katho, Archbishop of Venney, who, like himself, had never in the service first of the Duke of Burgundy, and afterwards in that of Louis XII; and it is also work that he is alone matched for the celebrity of his name. Indeed, among modern historians, no one has been estimated more likely than Comines, who, to the claim of a natural and flexible style, which were on the direct impress of his thoughts, and to the interest which belong to the fresh and annual central of an eye-tousness, unless a second bound knowledge of man and affairs, and displays cool observation in happy alliance with some judgment and concentrated determination. In estimating the qualities of conduct and the shades of character, Comines is perhaps entitled. Taking good as he found there, and regarding them merely as the instruments of Providence, he depicts them with a cool, rigorous, yet apparently un-studied severity, and so true do his delineations appear, that he seems to have looked into their very souls, and to have discovered the real principles or motives of which their actions were the necessary result or expression. We look in vain in his Memoirs for noble sentiments, chivalrous feelings, or lofty aspirations. He never rises above the level of his subject, nor sacrifices that calm dignity of tone which he sustains without effort, because it seems to have been natural to his character. He speaks little of himself; and the most important circumstances of his life are omitted, probably because the recital of them might have embarrassed him. The first edition of the Memoirs of Comines, published at Paris in 1525, contains only the reign of Louis XI from 1464 to 1484, and is divided into six books; but we none, containing the history of Charles VIII till the year 1498, appeared in 1528, Paris, folio. A new edition, however, revised and corrected, was published at Paris in 1552, folio, by the Sieur du Parc, and has often since been reprinted. Of modern editions, the most complete and valuable is that of Lengu University, London, 1747, 4 vols. 4to.
